title: Introduction to Bipartite Graph
description: Graphs whose nodes split into two groups with edges only crossing between them

blocks.text: A bipartite graph is one whose nodes can be split into two groups so that every edge connects a node in one group to a node in the other. No edge ever stays inside a single group.

This simple structure appears everywhere: students and courses, jobs and machines, buyers and sellers. Recognising that a graph is bipartite unlocks a whole family of matching and scheduling techniques.

blocks.caption: A bipartite graph: nodes split into two groups with edges only crossing between them
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655777-136540888.png

By the end of this topic you will know exactly what makes a graph bipartite, how to check it with a simple two coloring using BFS or DFS, why odd cycles are the deciding factor, and where this idea is used. It is one of the most useful classifications of a graph.
The idea is intuitive once you see it as two teams. Everyone belongs to one of two teams, and every relationship is a rivalry across teams, never a friendship within a team.
Formally, a graph is bipartite if its vertices can be divided into two disjoint sets, often called U and V, such that every edge has one endpoint in U and the other in V.

blocks.caption: Every edge crosses between the two groups; none stays within a group
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655777-701623079.png
The key restriction is that there are no edges within a group. Two nodes in the same set are never directly connected. All the connections cross from one side to the other.

items: The nodes split into two groups, U and V
Every edge goes from a node in U to a node in V
No edge connects two nodes in the same group
The two groups together contain all the nodes

blocks.text:
The mental picture:

Imagine two columns of nodes. Bipartite means every line you draw goes from the left column to the right column, and never connects two nodes in the same column.
As a quick example, a graph with edges A to 1, A to 2, B to 2, and C to 1 is bipartite with the letters in one group and the numbers in the other. No two letters connect, and no two numbers connect.

items: Two disjoint groups U and V hold all the nodes
Every edge has one end in U and the other in V
No edge connects two nodes inside the same group
Equivalent to being colorable with two colors

blocks.text: Bipartite graphs model any situation with two distinct kinds of things where relationships only cross between the kinds.

items: Students on one side and the courses they take on the other
Jobs on one side and the machines that can run them on the other
Applicants and the positions they apply to
Buyers and the products they purchase

blocks.text: In each case there is no meaningful edge within a group. Two students are not connected by taking a class; a student is connected to the class. That crossing only structure is exactly what bipartite captures.
Notice the common shape in all of these: two clearly different kinds of things, and every connection joins one kind to the other. That shape is the signal that a bipartite model fits.

items: Students and the courses they enroll in
Jobs and the machines able to run them
Applicants and the roles they apply for
Buyers and the products they purchase

blocks.text: There is a beautiful equivalent way to think about bipartite graphs: it is exactly the set of graphs you can color with two colors so that no edge joins two nodes of the same color.

blocks.caption: Two coloring: neighbors must differ in color, and success means the graph is bipartite
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655777-857625996.png
If you can paint every node either blue or green such that every edge connects a blue to a green, then the blues form one group and the greens form the other. That is precisely a bipartition.
This reframing is powerful because two coloring is something we can check mechanically by walking the graph, which turns an abstract property into a concrete algorithm.

Bipartite equals two colorable:

A graph is bipartite if and only if it can be properly two colored. Finding the coloring and finding the bipartition are the same task.

items: Paint each node one of two colors
Require that every edge joins two different colors
If you succeed, the two colors are the two groups
If you fail, the graph is not bipartite

blocks.text: This equivalence is the bridge from theory to code: instead of reasoning about abstract groups, you just try to two color the graph and see whether it works.
The standard way to test bipartiteness is a breadth first traversal that colors nodes as it goes. You start a node with one color, then color every neighbor the opposite color.

blocks.caption: BFS colors each level the opposite of the previous, alternating outward
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655777-590665340.png

As BFS spreads outward level by level, the colors naturally alternate: level zero is blue, level one is green, level two is blue, and so on. If you ever try to color a node and find a neighbor already has the same color, the graph is not bipartite.
Trace it on a simple path A to B to C. A is colored blue, B becomes green, C becomes blue again. No edge joins same colors, so this path is bipartite, as every path always is.

items: Color the start node and enqueue it
Give each uncolored neighbor the opposite color
If a neighbor already shares your color, stop and report false
Repeat across every component

blocks.text: Depth first search works just as well, and some find it cleaner. You color a node, then recurse into its neighbors, giving each the opposite color.
If a neighbor is uncolored, you color it and recurse. If it is already colored the same as the current node, an edge joins two same colored nodes, so the graph is not bipartite.
Both BFS and DFS visit every node and edge once, so pick whichever style you find clearer; the result is identical.
The recursion carries the opposite color down at each step. Because it explores one branch fully before backtracking, DFS is a natural fit when the graph is given recursively or is very deep.
One caution with DFS: on very large graphs the recursion can be deep, so an explicit stack or the BFS version avoids any risk of a stack overflow.
There is a clean theorem that tells you exactly when a graph fails to be bipartite: a graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no odd length cycle.

blocks.caption: Even cycles color cleanly; an odd cycle forces two neighbors to share a color
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655777-671822775.png

The reason is intuitive. As you walk a cycle alternating colors, an even length cycle returns to the start with the opposite color at each step and closes cleanly. An odd length cycle forces the last node to clash with the first.

items: No odd cycle means the graph is bipartite
Any odd cycle makes it impossible to two color
Even cycles are always fine and stay bipartite
This is why the coloring check detects a same color edge exactly on an odd cycle

blocks.text:
The single deciding factor:

Forget everything else and remember this: odd cycles are the only obstacle to being bipartite. No odd cycle, and the graph is bipartite.
A triangle is the smallest example. Its three nodes form a cycle of length three, which is odd, so no matter how you try to two color it, two of its nodes always end up the same color.
This is also why trees and forests are always bipartite. With no cycles at all, there can be no odd cycle, so a valid two coloring always exists.
A graph may come in several disconnected pieces, and a correct bipartite check must handle all of them, not just the piece containing your start node.

That is why the code loops over every node and starts a fresh traversal from any node that has not been colored yet. Each connected component is colored independently, and the whole graph is bipartite only if every component is.

items: A graph can have several disconnected components
Start a new traversal from every uncolored node
Each component is checked on its own
The graph is bipartite only if all components are

blocks.text:
Always loop over all nodes:

Wrap your traversal in an outer loop that starts from every uncolored node. This is the single most common correctness fix for bipartite checks.
Each component gets its own independent coloring, and a single failing component makes the entire graph non bipartite, even if all the others color perfectly.
The check is very efficient, since it is just a single traversal with a color assignment.

items: Time: O(V plus E), visiting every vertex and every edge once
Space: O(V) for the color array, plus the traversal queue or recursion stack
The same bound holds for both the BFS and DFS versions

blocks.text: This linear cost is why a bipartite check is cheap enough to run as a quick first step in many graph problems.
This is the same cost as a plain BFS or DFS, because the coloring adds only a constant amount of work per node and edge. Bipartiteness is essentially free to test.
Because it is only a linear pass, running a bipartite check as a quick screening step before a heavier algorithm costs almost nothing.
Knowing a graph is bipartite is not just a label; it opens the door to powerful algorithms that only apply to this structure.

items: Bipartite matching, pairing nodes on one side with nodes on the other
Assignment problems, like matching workers to tasks optimally
Certain scheduling problems where two kinds of resources alternate
Modeling and solving two coloring or two team partition questions

blocks.text: The most famous is maximum bipartite matching, which finds the largest set of pairings with no shared endpoints. It is solved with augmenting paths or by reduction to network flow.
Maximum bipartite matching is the headline result. It asks for the largest set of edges with no shared endpoints, which models assigning as many workers to distinct tasks as possible.

items: Maximum matching pairs up as many nodes as possible
Assignment problems find an optimal pairing
Vertex cover on bipartite graphs has efficient solutions
Two team or two group partitioning follows directly

blocks.text: Because so many real problems have two kinds of entities, bipartite models are everywhere.

items: Assigning jobs to workers or tasks to machines
Matching students to schools or projects
Detecting conflicts by splitting items into two compatible groups
Recommendation settings linking users and items

blocks.text: Whenever a problem naturally has two categories with relationships only between them, checking bipartiteness is a natural and often crucial first move.

items: Workers matched to tasks or shifts
Students matched to schools or projects
Ad slots matched to advertisers
Any two sided market linking one kind to another

blocks.text: The unifying theme is a two sided relationship. Once you spot two categories with only crossing links, a bipartite model and its matching algorithms usually apply.
A few mistakes trip people up when working with bipartite graphs.

items: Forgetting disconnected components: check must start from every uncolored node
Assuming connected: a graph can be bipartite in one part and be tested wrongly if you stop early
Self loops: an edge from a node to itself makes the graph non bipartite immediately
Confusing directions: bipartiteness is about the undirected structure, so treat edges as undirected when coloring

blocks.text:
The classic bug:

Running the coloring from a single start node and forgetting the outer loop over all nodes. Disconnected components will silently go unchecked.
Another subtle point: a graph with no edges at all is trivially bipartite, and so is any tree, since neither can contain a cycle, let alone an odd one.
Finally, remember to treat edges as undirected while coloring. Bipartiteness is a property of the undirected structure, even if the original graph was directed.
When a problem hints at two groups or a two way split, run through this.

items: Ask whether the entities fall into two kinds with edges only crossing between them
If so, model it as a graph and check bipartiteness by two coloring
Use BFS or DFS, coloring neighbors the opposite color, over all components
If an edge ever joins two same colored nodes, it is not bipartite, thanks to an odd cycle
If bipartite, consider whether a matching or assignment algorithm solves the real question

blocks.text: Framing a problem as bipartite is often the insight that turns a vague question into a known, solvable one.

Reframe first:

Many problems that never mention graphs are secretly bipartite checks in disguise. If you can split items into two conflicting groups, try coloring.

items: Identify two kinds of entities in the problem
Model crossing relationships as edges
Two color the graph across all components
If it colors cleanly, apply matching or assignment as needed

blocks.text: The bipartite property is a small idea that carries a lot of weight in graph problems.

items: A bipartite graph splits into two groups with edges only crossing between them
It is exactly the set of graphs that can be properly two colored
Check it with a BFS or DFS coloring in O(V plus E) time
A graph is bipartite if and only if it has no odd cycle
Bipartiteness unlocks matching, assignment, and scheduling algorithms

blocks.text: Whenever you spot two kinds of entities with crossing relationships, think bipartite, color the graph, and a whole toolkit opens up.
Hold on to one picture: two columns of nodes with every line crossing between them, and a two coloring that succeeds exactly when there is no odd cycle.
